Q6120.L3f: In inflation- and PPP-adjusted 2011 prices, the 1850 US was close to subsistence, with income per person near the level of a bare-minimum survival budget of about a dollar a day.
Q6120.L4f: The correct figure is that US GDP per capita in 1850 was only about three hundred dollars in 2011 prices.

Q5966.L1t: The heart pumps blood through its four chambers using coordinated electrical and mechanical activity.
Q5966.L2t: Systole is the phase in which the ventricles contract and eject blood, while diastole is the phase in which they relax and fill.
Q5966.L3t: The cardiac cycle is defined by the two alternating mechanical events of the heart, each named by a specific term, and there is no separate third named phase in the standard definition.
Q5966.L4t: The cardiac cycle consists of just two phases, diastole and systole.
Q5966.L2f: The cardiac cycle is timed entirely by the lungs, with each phase set by the breathing rate rather than by the heart's pacemaker.

Q5966.L4f: The cardiac cycle consists of contraction, relaxation, and rest.

Q6016.L1t: Glycolysis is the metabolic pathway that breaks glucose down into pyruvate in the cytoplasm of the cell.
Q6016.L2t: Glycolysis uses two ATP in the preparatory phase and produces four ATP in the payoff phase by substrate-level phosphorylation.
Q6016.L3t: Starting from glycogen, the first hexose is phosphorylated by phosphorylase using inorganic phosphate rather than ATP, so one fewer ATP is spent than when starting from free glucose.
Q6016.L4t: Glycolysis nets two ATP from glucose and three ATP from glycogen.
Q6016.L2f: Glycolysis takes place inside the mitochondrial matrix, where it is coupled directly to the electron transport chain.
Q6016.L3f: Glycogen entry into glycolysis costs no ATP at all and glucose entry costs one ATP, so the net yields are one apart, with glucose giving three and glycogen giving four.
Q6016.L4f: Glycolysis nets three ATP from glucose and four ATP from glycogen.

Q5651.L1t: Sales of goods such as automobiles are governed by Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code.
Q5651.L2t: Under the UCC, a seller's description of the goods, including in an advertisement, can become part of the basis of the bargain and create an express warranty.
Q5651.L3t: A disclaimer clause is inoperative to the extent it conflicts with an express warranty, and a clause saying goods are sold in their current condition excludes implied warranties but cannot undo the seller's specific promise about what the car is, here its model year.
Q5651.L4t: Carol should win, because the clause saying the car is sold in its current condition cannot cancel the seller's express promise that the car was a 1964 model.
Q5651.L2f: The UCC requires that every contract for the sale of a used car be notarized before it is enforceable.
Q5651.L3f: A seller is liable for misdescribing goods only if the buyer proves the seller was careless, because express warranty liability depends on fault.
Q5651.L4f: The seller wins unless Carol can show carelessness in how the picture was presented, so the contract language protects the seller otherwise.

Q5541.L1t: The Pew Research Center surveys attitudes toward religion and morality in many countries, including India.
Q5541.L2t: Pew's 2019 survey on belief in God and morality covered 34 countries, and India was among the countries where tying morality to belief in God was far more common than in Western Europe.
Q5541.L3t: Pew's 2019 figure for India was above three-quarters of respondents but well short of nine in ten.
Q5541.L4t: The share of Indians who say belief in God is necessary for morality is just under eighty percent, in the high seventies.

Q6064.L1t: Adverse possession is a property doctrine under which a possessor can acquire title to land after occupying it for a statutory period.
Q6064.L2t: More than twenty years passed between the landowner's death in 1986 and the Girl Scouts' discovery of their claim in 2009, so the 20-year period is long enough to have run if the other elements were met.
Q6064.L3t: Adverse possession requires possession that is hostile, meaning under a claim inconsistent with the true owner's rights, and a tenant who thinks he still holds under the owner's lease is not asserting a hostile claim.
Q6064.L4t: The Girl Scouts win if the tenant thought the lease continued, because possession under a supposed lease is not hostile and the adverse possession period never ran.
Q6064.L2f: In most states the adverse possession period starts to run only when the true owner learns that someone is occupying the land.
Q6064.L3f: When a tenant stops paying rent after the landlord dies, the lease ends at once and the owner's successor takes title, whatever the tenant's state of mind.
Q6064.L4f: The Girl Scouts win simply because the tenant stopped paying rent after the landlord died.

Q8166.L1t: Henry Maine was a 19th-century legal historian whose book Ancient Law examined how early legal systems developed.
Q8166.L2t: Maine's phrase appears in Ancient Law, where he contrasts societies organized by family-based status with those organized by individual agreements.
Q8166.L3t: Maine wrote the line as a description of what had happened in the societies he had studied up to then, as the word 'hitherto' signals, and he did not offer it as a rule about what would happen later.

Q8166.L2f: Maine published the aphorism in a 1950s essay on the law of contracts, written as a reply to Marxist critics of the legal system.
Q8166.L3f: Maine's own account of status was a loose, shifting one, covering any social position at all, from wealth and occupation to personal taste, which later writers had to narrow down.
Q8166.L4f: The aphorism is mainly misunderstood because readers distort what Maine meant by status, which he defined differently from how it is usually presented.

Q8178.L1t: Both the Roman Empire and Han China were large agrarian empires that expanded through conquest and kept their rule going with professional armies.
Q8178.L2t: Both empires had long trade networks, including the Silk Roads, that linked the Mediterranean world with East and South Asia.
Q8178.L3t: As the overland empires that guarded and funded the Silk Roads broke up, the roads became less safe and less profitable, so merchants turned increasingly to maritime routes across the Indian Ocean.
Q8178.L4t: The collapse of both empires pushed commerce away from the overland Silk Roads and toward Indian Ocean sea routes.
Q8178.L2f: After the Han dynasty fell, Chinese rulers sealed the empire's borders and banned all foreign trade for several centuries.

Q8118.L1t: The solar nebula was the cloud of gas and dust that collapsed to form the Sun and the planets about 4.6 billion years ago.
Q8118.L2t: Condensation in the solar nebula depended on temperature, so only metals and rocks could form solids in the hot inner region near the young Sun.
Q8118.L3t: Hydrogen and helium made up about 98 percent of the nebula's mass, which is more than all the heavier materials combined, and of those heavier materials the ices (hydrogen compounds) outweighed the rocks, which in turn outweighed the metals.
Q8118.L4t: Light gases come first by mass, followed by hydrogen compounds, then rocks, and metals come last.
Q8118.L2f: The solar nebula was a perfectly uniform cloud with the same composition at every distance from the Sun, and it did not rotate at all.
Q8118.L3f: Because the ices of water, methane and ammonia were so abundant everywhere, they outweighed even hydrogen and helium together, and the rocks and metals made up the smallest share.
Q8118.L4f: The correct ordering is light gases first, then hydrogen compounds, then metals, and rocks last.

Q8294.L1t: Water's phase diagram shows the solid, liquid and gas regions separated by equilibrium lines that meet at a triple point.
Q8294.L2t: The liquid-solid equilibrium line of water slopes backward (up and to the left), unlike that of most substances, which slope forward.
Q8294.L3t: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open, ordered crystalline lattice that packs them less densely than the liquid, so ice floats, and applying pressure favors the denser phase.
Q8294.L4t: The negative slope arises because ice is less dense than liquid water, owing to its hydrogen-bonded crystalline framework.
Q8294.L2f: The triple point of water lies at a pressure far above atmospheric pressure, so water at 1 atm can never exist as a gas.
Q8294.L3f: Solid water is less dense than liquid water, and it is low external pressure that pushes the solid to melt into liquid, which fixes the slope of the line.
Q8294.L4f: The negative slope is explained by ice being less dense than liquid water, which makes the solid turn into liquid under low pressure.

Q5100.L1t: Landowners and landlords can be held liable in negligence for injuries on or near their property, depending on the duty they owe and the foreseeability of harm.
Q5100.L2t: A landlord's liability for a third party's criminal act generally depends on whether the landlord had a duty to protect and whether the harm was a foreseeable result of conditions they could control.
Q5100.L3t: The owner knew of the tenant's drug dealing and of earlier violent confrontations including a gun discharge, so a shooting that endangers neighbors was a foreseeable risk that the owner could have reduced by evicting.
Q5100.L4t: The neighbor should recover because the owner knew of the danger created by the tenant's drug dealing and did nothing about it.
Q5100.L2f: Courts treat landlords as having no responsibility at all for conditions arising from tenants' activities once the lease has been signed and rent is being paid.
Q5100.L3f: Merely knowing that a tenant deals drugs, without any knowledge of violence, is by itself enough to make a landlord strictly liable for any injury connected to that tenant.
Q5100.L4f: The neighbor should recover simply because the owner knew that the tenant was dealing drugs from his apartment.

Q5365.L1t: Pet food brands in the United States use memorable advertising slogans and jingles to market their products to cat owners.

Q5365.L3f: The 'cats ask for it by name' claim belongs to the premium gourmet line that is marketed with elegant, upscale imagery and the word 'Feast' in its title.
Q5365.L4f: The brand that claims cats ask for it by name is Fancy Feast.

Q5672.L1t: Criminal law recognizes that a person who assists or commands another to commit a crime can be held liable as an accomplice or principal.
Q5672.L2t: Under the common law, an accessory's liability was traditionally derivative of the principal's guilt, though modern rules often allow trying the accessory separately.
Q5672.L3t: A defense based on the principal's personal incapacity or mental condition does not negate the crime itself, whereas a finding that the shooting was justified means no crime was committed at all, leaving nothing for the instigator to be liable for.
Q5672.L4t: The defendant can assert a valid defense if the man was acquitted because the killing was justified as protecting himself from the victim.
Q5672.L2f: At common law, an accessory before the fact could never be tried unless the principal had first been convicted of the same offense.
Q5672.L3f: An acquittal grounded on the principal's lack of mental capacity means the killing itself was lawful, so no crime was committed by anyone and the instigator cannot be liable.
Q5672.L4f: The defendant will be able to assert a valid defense if the man's acquittal was based on insanity.

Q5969.L1t: Homicide law distinguishes among murder, manslaughter, and non-criminal killings based on the defendant's mental state and conduct.
Q5969.L2t: The felony murder rule can make a death during a felony murder, and its reach includes the period of flight until the felon reaches a place of temporary safety.

Q5969.L4t: The defendant should not be found guilty of any crime for the child's death because it was an unavoidable accident.
Q5969.L2f: Involuntary manslaughter requires only that the death be caused by the defendant's act, with no need to show negligence or recklessness.
Q5969.L3f: Because the defendant was driving away from a robbery with stolen money and tequila, he was driving with a reckless disregard for others, so the death resulted from his own criminal negligence.
Q5969.L4f: The defendant should be found guilty of involuntary manslaughter for the child's death.

Q5233.L1t: The Apple iMac is a line of all-in-one desktop computers that has been sold in a range of designs since 1998.

Q5731.L1t: Future interests in property law include remainders and executory interests, which are classified by when and how they take effect.
Q5731.L2t: An estate pur autre vie is an estate whose duration is measured by the life of someone other than the holder.
Q5731.L3t: The brother's interest would cut short the uncle's life estate by taking effect on a condition (the uncle moving), and a future interest that divests a prior estate in this way, rather than waiting for it to end naturally, cannot be a remainder.
Q5731.L4t: Because the brother's interest takes effect by divesting the uncle's estate upon his move, it is a shifting executory interest.
Q5731.L2f: At common law, an estate pur autre vie could not be created by a deed and required a will to take effect.
Q5731.L3f: The brother's interest follows the prior estates and is subject to an uncertain condition precedent, and any future interest following a life estate that is not yet certain to vest is classified as a remainder.
Q5731.L4f: The brother's interest is best described as a contingent remainder because it depends on the uncertain event of the uncle moving.

Q5347.L1t: Skeletal muscle contraction is powered by energy from ATP, which is regenerated through several metabolic pathways.
Q5347.L2t: Muscle cells store only a small amount of ATP, and phosphocreatine and glycolysis supply additional energy as activity continues.
Q5347.L3t: The very first energy used in a brief maximal contraction is whatever is already present in the muscle and directly usable, before any regeneration pathway has had time to start.
Q5347.L4t: The initial energy for a very high force contraction lasting 1-2 seconds comes from the ATP already stored in the muscle.
Q5347.L2f: Muscle fibers hold large ATP reserves that can power maximal contractions for about a minute before other pathways are needed.
Q5347.L3f: Even in the first second of a maximal contraction, muscle ATP is used up almost instantly, so the first energy must come from breaking down glucose through the glycolytic pathway.
Q5347.L4f: The initial energy for a very high force contraction lasting 1-2 seconds comes from glycolysis.

Q5479.L1t: Inchoate crimes such as solicitation, attempt and conspiracy punish conduct that falls short of a completed target offense.
Q5479.L2t: At common law, conspiracy requires a genuine agreement between at least two persons who each intend to achieve the unlawful objective.
Q5479.L3t: Solicitation is complete the moment a person asks another to commit a crime with intent that it be committed, so later withdrawal does not undo it, but an agent who only feigns agreement and never intends to go through with the plan forms no true agreement.
Q5479.L4t: The wife is guilty of solicitation only, because her request was complete when made but no genuine agreement ever existed to make a conspiracy.
Q5479.L2f: Solicitation at common law is a form of attempt that requires the solicited crime to have actually been begun before liability attaches.
Q5479.L3f: A conspiracy is formed whenever one person proposes a crime and the other verbally assents, even if the assenting person is only pretending and secretly never intends to act.
Q5479.L4f: The wife is guilty of conspiracy to commit murder, because the agent's spoken agreement to the plan was enough to complete the conspiracy.

Q5849.L1t: The hearsay rules govern out-of-court statements offered to prove the truth of what they assert, and they include an exception for business records.
Q5849.L2t: The business records exception requires a foundation, usually from a custodian or other qualified witness, that the records were made at or near the time by someone with knowledge, kept in the regular course of business, and made as a regular practice.
Q5849.L3t: Records are out-of-court statements even when their maker testifies, and computer records need a showing that the process and inputs are reliable, which a bare statement that the records were kept regularly does not supply.
Q5849.L4t: The court will demand a fuller foundation showing the reliability of the computer records before admitting them.
Q5849.L2f: Computer-generated records were barred from evidence in federal courts altogether until a rules amendment in 2000 first allowed them.
Q5849.L3f: A statement falls outside the hearsay rule whenever the person who made it is present and available to testify at trial, regardless of when or where it was made.
Q5849.L4f: The hearsay objection fails because the defendant is the declarant and is available in court.

Q5735.L1t: Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction, and removal allows certain actions filed in state court to be moved to federal court.
Q5735.L2t: Removal is governed by 28 U.S.C. 1441, and a motion to remand based on a procedural defect in removal must be made within thirty days of the notice of removal.
Q5735.L3t: The removal statute gives the power to remove only to defendants, so a plaintiff who chose to sue in state court cannot remove her own case, even when it includes federal claims.
Q5735.L4t: The federal court will send the entire case back to state court because the plaintiff had no right to remove it.
Q5735.L2f: Removal of a federal-question case is allowed only if the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000.
Q5735.L3f: Any party to a state-court action, plaintiff or defendant, may remove it once a federal claim appears in the complaint, provided notice is filed within thirty days.
Q5735.L4f: The court will keep the case, because the removal was timely and the complaint includes federal claims.

Q5647.L1t: Ugg boots are woollen-lined sheepskin footwear that originated in Australia.
Q5647.L2t: Shane Stedman made his first sheepskin boots in 1973 and sold the rights to the US company Deckers in 1983.
Q5647.L3t: Stedman said that making the brand a world leader would mean moving to the US, which he refused to do because he would never give up Sydney and surfing, so he let the rights go without regret.
Q5647.L4t: The text mainly shows that the inventor willingly gave up a possible fortune so he could keep his life in Sydney and his surfing.
Q5647.L2f: Stedman sold the rights to Deckers in 1995 for a lump sum of one million pounds.
Q5647.L3f: The passage is chiefly about the purpose behind the boots' creation, which was to serve the surfing community alone, and the sale of the rights is only a minor detail.
Q5647.L4f: The text mainly tells us that the boots were created with surfers specifically in mind.

Q5649.L1t: Catheter valves are used with urinary catheters as an alternative to a drainage bag.
Q5649.L2t: A catheter valve is a tap-like device fitted to the end of a catheter that lets the bladder fill and then be emptied at intervals.
Q5649.L3t: A valve works by letting the bladder fill and then releasing urine at intervals, but just after surgery the bladder usually needs to stay continuously drained.
Q5649.L4t: A catheter valve would not be used for a patient who has just had surgery.

Q5649.L4f: You would avoid a catheter valve when there is no requirement to measure urine output.

Q8537.L1t: Philosophers of law debate both what punishment is and whether it can be morally justified.
Q8537.L2t: Definitions of punishment typically describe an authority deliberately inflicting unpleasant consequences on someone for an offence.
Q8537.L3t: If a moral justification were built into the definition, any argument over whether punishment is justified would be settled in advance by definition, so the definition must not presuppose any moral stance.
Q8537.L4t: Separating them matters so that the definition stays neutral on values, leaving moral justification to be argued as a separate question.
Q8537.L2f: The concept of punishment is generally agreed to have been fixed by Kant in a single, uncontested formulation.
Q8537.L3f: The reason for the separation is that punishment as an actual social institution runs independently of any moral reasons offered for it, so the two must not be run together.
Q8537.L4f: The separation matters because, in reality, the institution of punishment exists apart from any justification given for it.

Q6097.L1t: Property law distinguishes between present possessory estates such as the fee simple and the fee tail, and future interests such as reversions and remainders.
Q6097.L2t: A conveyance to a person "and the heirs of his body" traditionally created a fee tail, which is an estate limited to the grantee's lineal descendants.
Q6097.L3t: Most states today treat a fee tail as a fee simple, so the wife's cousin received the entire fee simple and the grantor kept no interest to pass on.
Q6097.L4t: The niece receives nothing, because the grantor had already given away his entire interest to the cousin and had nothing left to convey to her.
Q6097.L2f: A conveyance to a person "and the heirs of his body" traditionally created a life estate that automatically ended at the grantee's death, whatever his descendants did.
Q6097.L3f: Under modern law the cousin's estate is only a life estate or fee tail, so the grantor still holds the remaining future interest and can pass it to the niece by a later deed.
Q6097.L4f: The niece holds a fee simple in the property, because the later conveyance to her was effective and gave her full ownership.

Q8128.L1t: Chronic cough in adolescents can arise from airway, upper-respiratory, gastrointestinal, or cardiac causes, and the history and spirometry help sort them out.
Q8128.L2t: Chronic bronchitis is defined by a productive cough lasting at least three months in two consecutive years and is mostly seen in long-term smokers.
Q8128.L3t: The patient has a cough that appears only with exertion and resolves with rest, a sister with asthma, and normal baseline findings, which fits exercise-induced reversible airway narrowing in an atopic young person.
Q8128.L4t: The most likely diagnosis is asthma, specifically exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
Q8128.L2f: Chronic bronchitis is defined by a dry cough lasting a few days after a viral infection and is most often seen in young athletes.
Q8128.L3f: Chronic bronchitis is typically a cough that comes on with exercise in young non-smokers and goes away at rest, and it often runs in families, so this patient's features match it.
Q8128.L4f: The most likely diagnosis is chronic bronchitis, since the exercise-related cough points to it.

Q5583.L1t: Researchers studying social behavior often combine records, surveys, and observed patterns to support claims about when people make major life decisions.
Q5583.L2t: The study analyzed recent divorce filings in Washington State and found that divorce filings peak in March and August.
Q5583.L3t: The passage offers outside, indirect evidence that fits the authors' finding: online searches for divorce and child custody grow early in the year and reach their peak in March.

Q5583.L4f: The conclusion is supported by the statement that the divorce rate rises sharply in March and August.

Q5567.L1t: The Black Hills National Forest in South Dakota is a popular hunting area that draws many hunters in the autumn season.
Q5567.L2t: Mike Kintigh is a regional supervisor for the Game, Fish & Parks Department and commented on how often hunters go missing in the Black Hills.
Q5567.L3t: Kintigh explained that the Black Hills have many more roads than the Rocky Mountains, and that this is why getting lost there rarely lasts long, which implies the opposite is true of the Rockies.

Q5567.L2f: Kintigh said that the Game, Fish & Parks Department keeps a record of every hunter who has gone missing in the state's forests since the 1950s.

Q5567.L4f: Kintigh's words show that anyone who gets lost in the Black Hills is bound to spend a night in the woods.

Q6170.L1t: Global health agencies track the leading causes of death worldwide, and the rankings differ widely between rich and poor countries.
Q6170.L2t: Diabetes is a chronic condition in which the body cannot properly regulate blood sugar, and it is a major cause of death worldwide.
Q6170.L3t: Global Burden of Disease estimates for 2017 put dementia deaths at roughly 2.5 million per year, which is higher than the roughly 1.4 million deaths attributed to diabetes.
Q6170.L4t: Dementia caused more deaths worldwide than the other listed conditions in 2017.
Q6170.L2f: Diabetes deaths worldwide have been measured only in high-income countries, because poorer countries do not record the condition at all.
Q6170.L3f: Estimates for 2017 showed that diabetes caused about 4 million deaths globally each year, well above the figure for dementia, which was under 1 million.
Q6170.L4f: Diabetes caused more deaths globally than dementia in 2017, so diabetes is the right choice.

Q8442.L1t: Jurisprudence is the theoretical study of law, and legal scholars have long divided it into different schools and branches.
Q8442.L2t: Thomas Erskine Holland was an English jurist at Oxford who wrote The Elements of Jurisprudence, a widely used textbook in the late nineteenth century.
Q8442.L3t: The nineteenth-century jurist who delivered lectures on the Province of Jurisprudence Determined held that general jurisprudence deals with principles common to mature legal systems while particular jurisprudence deals with a single system, and he was the one who drew this line.
Q8442.L4t: John Austin was the jurist who recognized the distinction between general and particular jurisprudence.
Q8442.L2f: The Elements of Jurisprudence was first published in the 1500s and was written to describe the legal system of ancient Rome.
Q8442.L3f: The author of The Elements of Jurisprudence is the writer who first divided the subject into general jurisprudence for all legal systems and particular jurisprudence for a single one.
Q8442.L4f: Holland was the jurist who recognized the distinction between general and particular jurisprudence.

Q5004.L1t: Future interests such as executory interests follow a defeasible estate and can cut it short when a stated event occurs.
Q5004.L2t: The Rule Against Perpetuities voids a contingent interest unless it must vest or fail within a life in being at creation plus twenty-one years.
Q5004.L3t: The gift is to a class of the sister's children who reach 25, and the class can include children born long after the grant, and the church-use condition could be triggered at any remote time, so nothing guarantees the interest vests or fails within lives in being plus 21 years.
Q5004.L4t: The executory interest in the sister's children is void under the Rule Against Perpetuities, which leaves the friend holding the entire title.
Q5004.L2f: A general warranty deed covers only title defects that arose during the grantor's own period of ownership.
Q5004.L3f: The sister is a life in being, so every child she bears in her lifetime is counted, and the interest must vest or fail within her lifetime, which satisfies the Rule Against Perpetuities.
Q5004.L4f: The gift over to the sister's children is valid, so title is shared by the friend and every child the sister bears during her lifetime, whether or not already born.

Q6031.L1t: Happiness researchers compare self-reported well-being from large surveys across countries and across decades.
Q6031.L2t: Cross-national studies have compared how happy people say they are with how happy they believe others in their country to be.
Q6031.L3t: Survey data from the 1970s onward show that women's reported happiness in the United States fell in absolute terms and relative to men, while multi-country polling shows people in every country underestimating their compatriots' happiness.
Q6031.L4t: The first statement is true and the second statement is false.

Q6031.L4f: The first statement is false and the second statement is true.

Q5696.L1t: Popes have traditionally taken a regnal name on election, and many of these names are reused across the centuries.
Q5696.L2t: The most frequently used papal name is John, and many popes chose names to honor earlier popes or saints.
Q5696.L3t: The first successor of Peter was named Linus, a tenth-century pope reigned under the name Lando, and the name Leo was borne by thirteen popes, so three of the four names are accounted for.
Q5696.L4t: The name that no pope has ever held is the one that belonged to the martyred deacon and saint Lawrence.
Q5696.L2f: The custom of a pope adopting a new regnal name on election began only in the sixteenth century with Adrian VI.
Q5696.L3f: Leo was only ever used by antipopes and by saints who were never recognized as legitimate popes, so no true pope ever carried that name.
Q5696.L4f: Leo has never been the name of a pope, so it is the name that fits the question.

Q5115.L1t: Lactate is produced in skeletal muscle when pyruvate is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+.
Q5115.L2t: During exercise, the rate of glycolysis and the rate of pyruvate production can exceed the rate at which mitochondria oxidise pyruvate, so some pyruvate is diverted to lactate.
Q5115.L3t: At the onset of exercise, glycolytic flux rises rapidly while oxidative metabolism takes time to catch up, so pyruvate and NADH accumulate and pyruvate is reduced to lactate.
Q5115.L4t: Muscle lactate production rises when glycolysis is switched on at the start of exercise.
Q5115.L2f: Lactate dehydrogenase converts lactate to acetyl-CoA directly inside muscle cells, which is why it is found mainly in mitochondria.
Q5115.L3f: Lactate is formed from glucose breakdown only when the pathway cannot generate pyruvate, so blocking pyruvate formation is what pushes the muscle to make lactate.
Q5115.L4f: Muscle lactate production increases when pyruvate cannot be formed from glucose breakdown.

Q8288.L1t: Roger Williams was a 17th-century English Protestant minister who founded Rhode Island and argued for separating church and state.
Q8288.L2t: Puritans left England to practise their own religion freely, and in Massachusetts Bay they kept church membership and civil privileges tied to their own congregations, which Williams criticised.
Q8288.L3t: The passage criticises the civil state for imposing religion, and Williams was banished from Massachusetts because the Puritan colony itself did not tolerate dissenting beliefs and enforced its own orthodoxy.
Q8288.L4t: The Puritans meant religious freedom to cover themselves alone, not other groups.
Q8288.L2f: Puritan Massachusetts Bay was founded as a colony with a legally established policy of welcoming every religious group, and Williams was invited there as a guest preacher.
Q8288.L3f: Puritan colonial law granted religious liberty to every Christian denomination, including Catholics and Quakers, and banished only non-Christians.
Q8288.L4f: The Puritans believed religious freedom should be extended to all Christians.

Q5932.L1t: Intermittent high-intensity exercise such as football or sprint games draws heavily on both muscle glycogen and blood glucose as fuel.
Q5932.L2t: During prolonged intermittent high-intensity exercise, plasma adrenaline and other counter-regulatory hormones are elevated, and the liver supplies glucose to the blood.
Q5932.L3t: Intense bursts raise catecholamines, which stimulate hepatic glucose output beyond the rate at which working muscle takes glucose up, and muscle glycogen supplies much of the fuel.
Q5932.L4t: Blood glucose frequently rises by about 1 to 3 mM over this kind of exercise.
Q5932.L2f: Blood glucose in intermittent high-intensity exercise is regulated mainly by rising insulin secretion, which drives glucose from the blood into muscle throughout the session.
Q5932.L3f: In intermittent high-intensity exercise lasting 80-90 minutes, liver glycogen is exhausted and muscle uptake outstrips hepatic output, so blood glucose steadily declines.
Q5932.L4f: Blood glucose falls to hypoglycaemic levels during 80-90 minutes of intermittent high-intensity exercise.

Q8186.L1t: The song is a seventeenth-century German-language satire from the era of the Thirty Years' War, a conflict fought across central Europe.
Q8186.L2t: The "Winter King" was Frederick V, Elector Palatine, who accepted the Bohemian crown in 1619 after Bohemian nobles rejected Ferdinand.

Q8186.L4t: The narrator sides with the Habsburg emperor against the Protestant usurper, so the narrator most likely identifies as a Catholic.

Q8186.L3f: The song was written in a Balkan setting, and its scolding of the Winter King reflects loyalty to the Ottoman sultan, who was the real overlord of Bohemia and Prague.
Q8186.L4f: The narrator most likely identifies as a Muslim, since the song defends an Ottoman-backed claim to the Bohemian crown.

Q5149.L1t: Exchange rates, interest rates, and capital flows are linked, and each influences a country's trade balance and the demand for its currency.
Q5149.L2t: A higher real interest rate makes assets denominated in a country's currency more attractive to foreign investors seeking better returns.
Q5149.L3t: A higher real interest rate raises demand for dollars and appreciates the currency, which makes foreign goods cheaper for Americans and American goods more expensive abroad.
Q5149.L4t: The higher real interest rate raises the dollar's value, so U.S. imports increase.
Q5149.L2f: The trade deficit is the amount by which a country's exports exceed its imports, and it is unaffected by exchange rates in either direction.
Q5149.L3f: A higher real interest rate depreciates the dollar, because foreign investors sell U.S. assets, which makes U.S. goods cheaper abroad and imports costlier at home.
Q5149.L4f: The higher real interest rate leads to a decrease in the U.S. trade deficit.
